newsitem.title: FRANCE: French financial markets recover their nerve.
newsitem.headline: French financial markets recover their nerve.

text.p: After Monday's selling wave, French financial markets recovered their nerve on Tuesday following Prime Minister Alain Juppe's surprise announcement that he would quit even if the centre-right won re-election next weekend.

Shares were up nearly one percent at midday after the CAC-40 stock index plunged 3.9 percent on Monday -- its biggest one-day loss in four years -- following the left's upset win in the first round of the parliamentary vote.
The franc also firmed and bond prices were steady.
Analysts said they did not believe Juppe's decision to step down would boost the centre-right's chances in next Sunday's final vote, saying it smacked too much of panic in the centre-right coalition.
But, said one share analyst, "People just figure even if it is the left in power, they will have to follow the discipline imposed by world financial markets."
The blue-chip CAC-40 index tumbled 0.71 percent at the open, but retraced its losses to trade 0.81 percent or 21.50 points higher at 2,662.78 at 1130 GMT.

Fears the bourse could be in for another rough day after British traders returned to their desks following a long weekend failed to materialise although the market was still waiting for the opening of New York which was also on holiday on Monday.
Traders said French shares were up in line with other European bourses on the back of Wall Street's record close and that domestic buyers were back in the market.
"Other European markets continue to rise and on the other hand, right or left, (what is happening) is not the end of the world," a dealer said.

Shares in defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, rallied 2.45 percent to 175.50 francs after falling on Monday amid fears its privatisation could be scrapped by a Socialist administration. Other privatisation stocks also recovered, such as bank Credit Lyonnais, which soared 7.66 percent to 229 francs.
"There were fears the privatisation programme would have to be stopped but there is a growing realisation a Socialist-led government will also have to sell shares," said one trader.
"The amounts involved are considerable and they will need it for their budget.
The French franc rallied from Monday's low of 3.3784 against the German currency to trade at 3.3757 per mark.

One foreign exchange trader in Paris called the currency market "astonishingly calm. Of course, it could be that the market is not entirely free but we still haven't seen the hand of the Bank of France" buying up francs to support the currency.
Bond and interest futures rose on Juppe's plans announced late on Monday to resign after the second round vote on June 1 but selling by non-residents knocked them from their highs.

"The main point today for people coming back from holiday is they're seeing the headlines in the press the left could win," Morgan Stanley economist Eric Chaney said. "In this regard, Juppe's decision is small fry."

The June bond future contract was trading up 0.4 basis points at 128.34, after plunging 68 points on Monday. The yield premium on French assets was steady at minus 10 late on Monday after falling from minus 14 before Sunday's vote.

Analysts said the bond market would probably continue to be cushioned by domestic investors. They took advantage of the rise in yields after the first round result to buy French bonds all along the curve.

Merrill Lynch market strategist Joanne Perez said investors believed that "one way or another way we are going to get" to European monetary union but cautioned that the real issue was under what conditions.
President Jacques Chirac, who called the vote in a bid to win a free hand in the run-up to monetary union was due to address the country in a televised speech at 1800 GMT.
But analysts were sceptical that Chirac could rescue the centre-right's chances.

Juppe's decision to resign was "a step in the right direction but far too late, it emphasises the disarray. Why is Juppe unpopular? Not because he's a horrible man but because of the measures the government has introduced," said BZW bond analyst Phyllis Reed.
